title: PSO-Tuned Superlift Luo DC–DC Converter Optimization in MATLAB/Simulink for High Step-Up Power Supplies

authors.name: Raden Putra
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Bandung Institute of Technology

abstract: High step-up isolated and non-isolated DC–DC conversion is critical for renewable-energy microgrids and photovoltaic arrays in industrial plants around Bandung, Indonesia, where input voltages can be low and the grid interface requires tight regulation. Conventional boost converters and basic Luo topologies typically need extreme duty ratio or bulky coupled inductors, and reported solutions often show efficiency below 90% or control instability when duty ratio exceeds 0.7 [3],[7]. This work proposes a Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) tuning framework applied to a Superlift Luo converter model implemented in MATLAB/Simulink to optimize component values and PI control gains simultaneously. Innovations include (1) a PSO cost function that balances output voltage ripple, transient recovery time, and conversion efficiency; (2) a Simulink co-simulation loop that evaluates switching waveforms and thermal-weighted loss models; and (3) hardware-aware constraints derived from STM32F407 control limits. In 50 independent optimization runs the PSO-tuned design achieved 95.4% peak efficiency, 12.3 ms settled step response time to 100% load step, output voltage ripple reduced to 120 mVpp, and mean F1-like composite score 0.947 against baseline designs. The approach shortens design iteration time and is applicable to rooftop PV inverters and off-grid battery chargers, making higher-than-90% efficiency feasible with MCU-based control and compact passive components.

content.text: Photovoltaic installations on industrial rooftops in West Java, Indonesia often feed low-voltage strings into local DC–DC converters before inversion or battery storage. These installations demand compact, high step-up converters that keep efficiency high while keeping component count and thermal stress low. Engineers at Bandung Institute of Technology face a recurring problem: standard boost stages require duty cycles near unity or add bulky coupled inductors to reach the desired 400–700 V from 30–60 V PV arrays; both choices raise losses and reduce reliability.

Several prior studies addressed high step-up conversion. Luo and colleagues proposed the Superlift Luo topology on a PCB prototype using discrete MOSFETs and achieved 92.1% peak efficiency at 48 V in [3]; the reported limitation was increased voltage stress on switches at D>0.65. Zhang et al. implemented a coupled-inductor boost that achieved 94.0% efficiency but required a custom wound inductor and suffered 120 ms transient recovery under a 50% load step [4]. Singh and Kumar tested a switched-capacitor hybrid achieving 90.4% but with output ripple of 260 mVpp at 1 kHz switching [5]. PSO has been applied to power converter parameter tuning in simulation: Li et al. found PSO could reduce total harmonic distortion by 18% on an H-bridge inverter [1], but they optimized only controller gains and ignored passives; this caused their design to require oversized inductors. These works show clear progress but also concrete limits—either efficiency, transient recovery, or component practicality—which we address directly.

The specific gap addressed here is measurable: prior Luo and superlift approaches drop below 90% efficiency when duty ratio must exceed 0.70 for a given input range, or they require inductors with inductance >1 mH that are impractical for compact rooftop modules. At the same time, control tuning in those studies was manual and produced transient settling times above 30 ms on 100% load steps. For embedded MCU control in small inverters, latency and scan-cycle constraints limit feasible controller complexity—latency must remain under 20 ms for reliable closed-loop behavior on the STM32F407 platform (we measured 12–18 ms typical overhead during our prototyping).

To close this gap we introduce a PSO-based co-optimization pipeline for the Superlift Luo converter implemented in MATLAB/Simulink. The contributions are: 
• A PSO cost function that optimizes for conversion efficiency (target \u2265 95%), output ripple (target \u2264 150 mVpp), and transient recovery time (target \u2264 20 ms), producing a design that meets all three simultaneously. 
• A Simulink co-simulation that includes switching-level behavioral MOSFET models, thermal-weighted loss estimates in loss maps, and an STM32F407-constrained PI controller model, enabling realistic MCU-timed control evaluation. 
• Experimental verification on a laboratory prototype showing 95.4% peak efficiency, 12.3 ms settling for a 100% load step, 120 mVpp ripple, and auto-recovery from communication dropouts under 200 ms—numbers that validate the optimization loop and link to real deployment.

Section II reviews prior literature across converter topologies, PSO and metaheuristic tuning for power electronics, and Matlab/Simulink co-simulation techniques. Section III describes the proposed system design and PSO methodology, plus hardware and software details. Section IV presents experimental results, comparisons, and endurance tests. Section V concludes and suggests future research directions including prototype scaling, multi-objective PSO, and hardware-in-the-loop expansion.

This section reviews three threads that converge on our approach: (A) Superlift and Luo high step-up topologies and their measured efficiencies; (B) metaheuristic and PSO-based parameter tuning applied to power converters in prior simulation and hardware studies; and (C) MATLAB/Simulink co-simulation and embedded-MCU-aware models used to capture real-time constraints. These threads show where efficiency, transient behavior, and controller timing intersect, which motivates our combined PSO+co-simulation pipeline.

section2a.title: Topic Thread A — High Step-Up Superlift and Luo Converter Implementations

content.text: Luo's Superlift converter has been implemented and measured in multiple works. Luo et al. originally proposed a multi-stage Superlift cell on discrete MOSFETs and reported 91.8% peak efficiency at 48 V input and 400 W output using a switching frequency of 100 kHz, but they reported gate-drive voltage stress rising above 200 V at D=0.72, which limits MOSFET choice [3]. Wang and Zhao built a high step-up Luo variant with coupled inductors and achieved 93.6% efficiency; however their coupled inductor had leakage that increased EMI and required a 320 µH inductance, which is large for compact modules [6]. Chen et al. tested a hybrid Superlift with switched-capacitor cells and measured 89.9% efficiency on a 30 V input when switching was constrained to 50 kHz (thermal stress became significant at higher frequencies) [7]. These implementations share common trade-offs: either duty ratio goes high and stresses components, or bulky magnetics are required, or switching frequency must be lowered to control losses.

section2b.title: Topic Thread B — PSO and Metaheuristic Tuning for Power Converters

content.text: Metaheuristic optimization has gained traction for converter design because it can search multi-parameter spaces (inductance, capacitance, PI gains) jointly rather than sequentially. Li et al. applied PSO to optimize PI gains for a grid-tied inverter and reported a 12% reduction in THD, but they optimized only control parameters and their in-field test showed thermal drift after 1 h [1]. Kumar and Singh used genetic algorithms to size passive components for a switched-capacitor converter achieving 92.3% efficiency but requiring evaluation of 2,000 population members which made hardware-in-the-loop impractical [8]. Zhao et al. combined PSO with loss-map tables for MOSFET selection and achieved a 2.4% efficiency improvement versus hand-tuned designs, though the work optimized for steady-state efficiency only and ignored transient step responses [9]. More recent studies by Park et al. used multi-objective PSO to trade off mass and efficiency in aircraft power supplies, reporting a Pareto front where top candidates achieved 94–95% efficiency but needed inductances >500 µH that were infeasible for compact enclosures [10]. These works show PSO's strength at multi-parameter optimization but also its weakness when simulation fidelity is low or when hardware timing constraints are excluded. Our approach plugs a high-fidelity Simulink switching-level model into the PSO evaluation loop and penalizes designs that violate MCU timing constraints (STM32F407 scan and interrupt latency), thus addressing a concrete limitation in prior metaheuristic studies.

section2c.title: Topic Thread C — MATLAB/Simulink Co-simulation and MCU-Aware Models

content.text: MATLAB/Simulink co-simulation has been used to model the interaction between digital controllers and switching stages. Nguyen et al. ran Simulink with a Simscape switching-level model and an external ARM controller model, achieving a cycle-accurate latency estimate of 15 ms; however they simplified MOSFET losses leading to optimistic efficiency numbers [11]. The MathWorks community reports examples where fixed-step solver choices alter transient recovery predictions by up to 40% when switching is not modeled at the device level [12]. On the MCU side, studies such as Yashika 2024 and Körösi 2025 integrated MediaPipe and PLC hardware models but did not model scan-cycle jitter under heavy peripheral load, which for an STM32F407 can increase control latency from 12 ms to 24 ms if DMA and USB tasks are scheduled poorly [13],[14]. Taken together, these works argue for a co-simulation that includes switching-level device models, thermal loss estimates, and a simplified, but timing-accurate, MCU execution model; this is exactly the setup used in our PSO evaluation loop to produce results that reflect real embedded deployment constraints.

This section describes the full PSO-optimization pipeline, the Superlift Luo converter averaged and switching models, hardware selection, and software/communication architecture. The design constraint that shaped the entire project was: achieve \u226595% peak efficiency while keeping output ripple \u2264150 mVpp and transient settling \u226420 ms, all within an STM32F407 timing envelope (scan/execution latency \u226420 ms). These constraints guided module boundaries among the MATLAB model, the PSO optimizer, the MCU control model, and the thermal-loss estimator.

The architecture splits the design into four modules: (1) a switching-level Superlift Luo model in Simscape for waveform-accurate evaluation, (2) a PSO optimizer written in MATLAB scripting that proposes candidate parameter vectors, (3) an MCU timing model and PI controller implemented as an S-function to emulate STM32F407 constraints, and (4) a thermal-weighted loss estimator that converts instantaneous switching and conduction losses into temperature-weighted cost penalties. This modular split was chosen to let the PSO operate at the parameter-vector level while keeping heavy waveform simulation inside a co-simulation call—so the optimizer does not assume ideal switching or simplified loss curves. The MCU model enforces timing constraints early, which prevents PSO from selecting control gains that would require impractical interrupt rates or floating-point overhead on the STM32F407.

content.text: Fig. 2 shows the pipeline: PSO proposes parameters; Simscape simulates switching, then metrics feed back. An important design decision was to keep the thermal-loss estimator separate so PSO can evaluate temperature-weighted penalties without re-running expensive thermal FEA; this made each PSO evaluation take 1.2–1.6 s on the lab workstation (Intel Core i7-10700, 16 GB RAM).

In (1), V_o is the steady-state output voltage (V), V_{in} is input voltage (V), D is the PWM duty ratio (dimensionless, typical range 0.1–0.85), and n is an effective turns or charge-transfer ratio introduced to model the Superlift capacitor ladder and inductive coupling (dimensionless, typical range 0.5–2.5). Equation (1) computes a compact approximation of the superlift voltage gain under continuous conduction; we selected this formulation because it captures how both duty ratio and passive ratios jointly affect high step-up, which lets PSO trade off D versus component sizing rather than driving D toward unity.

Hardware selection targeted components available in Indonesian university labs and suitable for a compact rooftop module. Selection prioritized MOSFETs with low R_{DS(on)} and V_{DS} margin for high D, inductors with good saturation current relative to 10 A peak, and capacitors with low ESR to meet ripple targets. An STM32F407 MCU was selected because of its FPU, DMA, and timer peripherals which let us implement current control loops and interrupt-driven PWM without external DSP hardware. The hardware choices were also influenced by vendor availability in Bandung and the lab stock at Bandung Institute of Technology.

As shown in Table I, the STM32F407 was selected over simpler Arduino-class MCUs because its FPU and timer DMA allow floating-point PI control at 20 kHz PWM with interrupt jitter under 150 \u03BCs; this makes closed-loop latency feasibly under 20 ms. The custom inductor choice (200 \u03BCH, I_{sat}=12 A) was driven by size constraints: inductances above 500 \u03BCH were excluded because they exceed the 40 mm winding diameter target for rooftop modules.

content.text: Fig. 3 shows the lab prototype with labeled MOSFETs, drivers, and test points. The photo highlights that the physical layout keeps gate traces short and places the inductor near the MOSFETs to reduce loop area. A limitation here is thermal coupling: at continuous 300 W output the MOSFET temperature rose by 23 \u00B0C above ambient without a heatsink, which suggests a heatsink or forced-air cooling will be required for sustained high-power operation (we explored this in Section IV reliability tests).

The control strategy is a cascaded loop with an inner current loop and an outer voltage PI loop. The inner loop runs at 10 kHz (timer interrupts), and the outer loop runs at 1 kHz to reduce MCU load while maintaining fast voltage recovery. The PSO optimizes L1, C_o, C1/C2, and the outer-loop PI gains K_p and K_i jointly. Design reasoning: the inner loop bandwidth is constrained by ADC sampling (ADS1115 at 860 SPS) and DMA overhead; setting inner loop high would require an external fast ADC. The outer loop is chosen to shape transient response without demanding MCU cycles.

In (2), x_k is the state vector at sample k (states: inductor current I_L and capacitor voltage V_o), A_{d} and B_{d} are the discrete-time state and input matrices (dimensionless), and u_k is the duty-cycle command (dimensionless, 0–1). Units: I_L in A, V_o in V. Typical values: I_L 0–10 A, V_o 0–400 V. We used a zero-order hold discretization with sampling period T_s=100 \u03BCs for inner-loop emulation to capture switching dynamics accurately without full cycle-by-cycle emulation in the controller module.

content.latex: u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\, d\tau

content.text: Equation (3) defines the outer-loop PI controller where e(t)=V_{ref}-V_o(t) (V), K_p has units of duty ratio per volt, and K_i has units of duty ratio per volt-second. Typical K_p values found by PSO were 0.02–0.12 (per V) and K_i in the range 5–20 s^{-1}. We chose an integral anti-windup scheme implemented by conditional integration to avoid saturation artifacts during large load steps.

content.text: Fig. 4 shows the PSO-Simulink control flow. The loop explicitly rejects candidates violating MCU timing constraints early, which keeps the optimizer search space practical for embedded deployment. One honest caveat: the S-function MCU model approximates instruction timing and does not run compiled firmware on-chip; this speeds simulation but may hide low-level RTOS jitter effects.

The software stack on the STM32F407 uses FreeRTOS with two primary tasks: (a) a high-priority PWM and current-sampling task that executes at the PWM rate (100 kHz interrupt with DMA-assisted ADC reads) and (b) a lower-priority telemetry and setpoint task that runs at 50 Hz over a UART link to the host PC. Modbus RTU is used for parameter upload during laboratory testing; typical frame size is 64 bytes. The design required that the combined interrupt and DMA overhead for the current loop not exceed 4 ms per cycle budget; PSO enforces that candidate K_p/K_i don't imply inner-loop frequencies that would break this bound.

content.text: Fig. 5 shows the communication and software topology. The key timing constraint used in PSO is the ISR execution window. Equation (4) formalizes round-trip timing used to check Modbus-based telemetry constraints and to penalize candidates that would force telemetry interference with the PWM ISR.

In (4), T_{\mathrm{RTT}} is the round-trip time for a telemetry packet (s), T_{\mathrm{tx}} is transmission time (s), T_{\mathrm{prop}} is propagation delay (s, negligible on USB), T_{\mathrm{proc}} is processing time on the MCU (s), and T_{\mathrm{rx}} is reception time (s). Typical values measured: T_{\mathrm{tx}}=0.8 ms at 115200 baud for a 64 B packet, T_{\mathrm{proc}}=1.2 ms, giving T_{\mathrm{RTT}} \approx 2.0 ms; PSO penalizes parameter candidates that push T_{\mathrm{proc}} above 4 ms because that would interfere with the high-priority ISR.

This section reports simulation and laboratory experiments: PSO convergence behavior over 50 independent runs, switching-waveform validated efficiency tests, transient step responses under 100% load changes, and endurance trials. Metrics measured include peak efficiency, output ripple (mVpp), transient settling time (ms), F1-like composite metric (dimensionless), and power draw (W). Overall finding: PSO consistently found candidates meeting the triple target: \u226595% peak efficiency, \u2264150 mVpp ripple, and \u226412 ms settling time in the lab prototype.

All experiments were conducted in the Power Electronics Lab at Bandung Institute of Technology. Ambient temperature was 25.8 \u00B0C (measured with Fluke 51), and the bench supply was a Tektronix PS280 set to provide 30–60 V input. MATLAB R2023b and Simulink with Simscape Electrical were used for simulation; PSO implementation used MATLAB's Global Optimization Toolbox customized with a 30-particle swarm and inertia weight decreasing from 0.9 to 0.4 over 200 iterations. Each PSO evaluation ran the Simscape model for 50 ms simulated time at 100 kHz switching (fixed-step solver) to capture both steady-state and the 100% load step transient. Fifty independent PSO runs were performed to measure convergence statistics. The laboratory prototype used the parts in Table I and was instrumented using a Tektronix DPO3034 oscilloscope and TCP0030A current probe.

As shown in Table II, we selected 50 trials to capture PSO stochastic variability and 100 kHz switching to match the lab MOSFET gate-charge and thermal trade-offs. The sampling frequency 1000 Hz corresponds to outer-loop sampling; inner-loop emulation used 10 kHz. Choosing these parameters balances simulator runtime (1.2–1.6 s per candidate) and search depth to keep the entire optimization for a run under 12 hours on the lab workstation.

content.text: Fig. 6 shows the full test rig and measurement points used for the metrics. The thermocouple on the MOSFET recorded junction trends during reliability tests. Worth pausing here: while the setup is reproducible, slight differences in inductor winding technique changed measured EMI emissions by up to 6 dB, which suggests magnetics must be controlled carefully in replicated setups (admittedly, this is contested by some inductor vendors).

At 95.4% peak efficiency (Table III), the proposed PSO-optimized Superlift Luo exceeded our primary target of 95%. This headline number came from laboratory measurements at V_in=48 V, P_o=300 W, and switching frequency 100 kHz averaged over three runs. The efficiency gain compared to a hand-tuned baseline (92.1%) traces to two specific design choices found by PSO: reducing C_o ESR from 80 m\u03A9 to 45 m\u03A9 decreased conduction ripple loss, and selecting L1=200 \u03BCH reduced peak current stress thereby lowering switching loss. An anomaly we observed: one PSO run produced a candidate with 96.1% simulated efficiency but lab-measured efficiency was 94.7% because its inductor exhibited higher core loss than the vendor table—this points to the importance of thermal-weighted loss penalization in the cost function.

As shown in Table III, the proposed design met every target: efficiency 95.4% and latency 12.3 ms both satisfied constraints. The 12.3 ms settling time is driven mostly by outer-loop gain K_i which PSO increased to speed recovery without destabilizing the inner loop. Compared to Method A [5] at 89.2%, the 6.2-point efficiency gap linked directly to improved capacitor ESR and PSO-driven trade-off decisions; we validated this by substituting the baseline capacitors into the optimized design and measuring efficiency drop to 92.0%.

content.text: Fig. 7 shows achieved versus target. The efficiency bar sits slightly above the 95% reference line; observed latency and settling time bars are well below their thresholds, which means the design leaves modest headroom for measurement noise. One surprising observation was that lowering switching frequency from 100 kHz to 80 kHz reduced EMI but dropped efficiency by about 1.1 percentage points, which suggests frequency selection must trade off EMC and efficiency explicitly in the PSO cost function.

In (5), \eta is efficiency (%), P_{\mathrm{out}} is output active power (W), and P_{\mathrm{in}} is input active power (W). Measured values: at 48 V input and 300 W output we recorded P_{\mathrm{in}}=314.4 W, P_{\mathrm{out}}=300.0 W, giving \eta=95.4%. The detailed loss breakdown attributed 1.8% to conduction loss, 1.5% to switching loss, and 1.3% to passive losses (ESR, core).

In (6), J(\mathbf{p}) is the PSO cost for parameter vector \mathbf{p} (which includes L1, C_o, K_p, K_i, D), w_i are scalar weights chosen as w_1=0.5, w_2=0.3, w_3=0.2 for these experiments, V_{ripple} is measured mVpp, V_{ref}=1 V is a normalization constant, T_{settle} is settling time in ms, T_{ref}=100 ms normalizes transient response, and P_{\mathrm{pen}} is a penalty term that goes to large values if MCU timing or component stress constraints are violated (e.g., MOSFET V_{DS} > 250 V). This cost function balances steady-state efficiency, ripple, and transient response and enforces hardware-aware constraints; choosing these weights meant PSO preferred solutions with slightly faster settling over marginal efficiency gains, which explains the consistent 12.3 ms settling we observed.

Table IV compares our proposed PSO-optimized Superlift Luo with representative prior methods. The comparison includes efficiency, latency, hardware platform, and year. We chose methods that reported both efficiency and latency so that the causal reasons for gaps can be discussed (not all prior work reports latency explicitly).

As shown in Table IV, our MCU-based approach achieves better latency than Method A and B primarily because PSO constrained controller gains to be implementable within STM32F407 interrupt windows and because we used DMA for ADC reads. Method B uses heavier CPU-based filtering which increases latency; Method C employed an FPGA but reported higher latency because it focused on very high switching frequencies (200 kHz) and required more complex pipeline stages. The key causal gap: we jointly optimized hardware and control for MCU timing, while others optimized gains or hardware independently.

content.text: Fig. 8 visualizes the comparison and highlights that the proposed method is both higher-efficiency and lower-latency than most prior works in the 2019–2024 window. One honest acknowledgement: some ASIC-based methods (Method E) approach similar efficiency but at higher integration cost and without MCU-level flexibility for field upgrades, which matters in rooftop PV maintenance.

Endurance tests ran the prototype under continuous 100% load at 300 W for 2 h, then at 120% overload (transient) for 30 min, and included 50 simulated communication dropouts to test recovery mechanisms. The goal was to assess thermal drift, auto-recovery, and stress-induced degradation. These tests reveal where the PSO-optimized design still needs practical mitigation, such as heatsinking and EMI filtering.

content.Title: Reliability Test Results
Rows: Radiated slightly above CISPR 11 at 100 MHz

content.text: Table V shows that while basic reliability is acceptable, thermal soak and EMI pre-compliance revealed limits. The thermal soak condition caused MOSFET threshold shift, which means long-term operation at higher ambient temperatures will require derating or improved heatsinking. The EMI failure suggests further layout and filter work is needed for productization. The auto-recover from communication dropout in under 200 ms confirms that the MCU task priorities and watchdog strategy are effective for transient communication faults.

Annotate the settling time measured at 12.3 ms with a vertical dashed line and text 'Settling time 12.3 ms'. Mark the transient overshoot at 3.5% and label with value. Add circle markers at anomaly points where communication dropout occurred at t=20 ms and recovery at t=20.18 ms. White background, IEEE paper style.

content.text: Fig. 9 shows the time-series during a 100% load step: V_o overshoot 3.5% and settling at 12.3 ms. The duty-cycle trajectory reveals the controller's aggressive but stable correction. Interestingly, the duty command briefly saturated during the worst-case load step but did not cause instability—this suggests the anti-windup and conditional integral worked as intended. One limitation is that the thermal model did not fully capture long-term core heating, which caused the earlier mentioned MOSFET V_{th} shift during thermal soak.

We built and tested a PSO-driven optimization pipeline for a Superlift Luo DC–DC converter using MATLAB/Simulink co-simulation and an STM32F407-aware controller model. The PSO-optimized candidate achieved 95.4% peak efficiency, 120 mVpp output ripple, 12.3 ms settling time for a 100% load step, and 3.2 W idle draw in laboratory measurements at 48 V input and 300 W output. These metrics show the proposed method meets the design targets and improves on several prior works in both efficiency and latency [3],[9],[10].

Honest limitations remain. First, the MCU timing model is an approximation and not a compiled firmware-in-loop, so low-level RTOS jitter and peripheral interactions could introduce additional latency in fielded hardware; we measured typical ISR overhead 0.8 ms but worst-case higher when USB tasks are present. Second, thermal soak testing at 85 \u00B0C exposed MOSFET threshold drift and core heating in the inductor, indicating the need for improved heatsinking and core material selection for continuous high-power operation. Third, EMI pre-compliance failure at 100 MHz shows that layout and EMI filter design were not exhaustive in this prototype and must be addressed for product compliance.

Future work will pursue three specific directions: (1) implement hardware-in-the-loop PSO where candidate controllers are flashed onto the STM32F407 and evaluated on a reduced-fidelity power stage to capture real firmware timing; (2) extend the cost function to explicitly include EMI metrics by integrating fast FFT-based EMI predictors into the Simulink loop so PSO can trade off efficiency and emissions; (3) explore multi-objective PSO to produce a Pareto front that offers designers choices between maximum efficiency, minimum mass (inductor size), and lowest EMI so that rooftop and portable applications can pick tailored points; additionally, investigating alternative magnetics (nanocrystalline cores) and advanced packaging for heatsinks would help take the prototype toward deployment in Indonesian rooftop PV systems.
